title: Roma's Review: Ragtime
transcript: Roma Torre: As I stand here outside Lincoln Center, I am surrounded by people chasing the American dream. The guy rushing to work; someone pushing a child to daycare, perhaps, or a kid racing to school. Meanwhile, inside, the Vivian Beaumont Theater up there, that exact chase plays out every night, eight times a week, on stage. Each of the musical’s many characters seeking stability, safety, a shot. Some make it, others are crushed by the system that simply tells them, work hard. That gap between promise and reality is why audiences leave the theater cheering, applauding simultaneously. The story is more than a century old, but it really is us right now. Originally, this revival was supposed to run just 14 weeks, but Lear deBessonet, the director, has such a hit on her hands, it was extended into the month of June. That gives you a little more time to get seats to this epic splendor. Now here is my review of Ragtime the Musical. (Music) Based on E.L. Doctorow’s classic 1975 historical novel and adapted for the stage by book writer Terrence McNally, along with composer Stephen Flaherty and lyricist Lynn Ahrens, Ragtime is truly timeless. This nearly flawless Lincoln Center Theater production ranks among Broadway’s best of all time. (Music) With that rousing opening number featuring the entire company, as if in a moving American tapestry, we’re introduced to each of the main characters. There are so many of them, in lesser hands, they’d be reduced to stereotype, or simply lost in the shuffle. But here, so masterfully staged by director deBessonet and choreographer Ellenore Scott, the combined effect of music, story, and performance on that mostly bare stage is breathtaking, and it left audiences cheering and weeping right from the start. Doctorow’s story begins in 1902, when ragtime music symbolized a turning point in the country, weaving the fates of Americans, Black and white, with the newly arrived huddled masses. McNally’s book focuses the complex tale on three sets of families. We first meet the affluent family in suburban New Rochelle, led by Father, the excellent Colin Donnell, and Mother, beautifully played by Caissie Levy, with a warmth and strength that puts an indelible stamp on the role. Then there are the folks from Harlem, the ragtime musician, Coalhouse Walker Jr. With his colossal pipes and commanding presence, Joshua Henry seems born to the role of the doomed character. It is a magnificent performance, and one that must not be missed. Together with the astonishing Nichelle Lewis as his lover, Sarah, the two will break your heart. The immigrants are represented by the Jewish Tateh and his young daughter, newly arrived from Latvia. Brandon Uranowitz delivers another extraordinary performance and a high mark in the fine actor’s career. Other key roles include real-life figures, union organizer Emma Goldman, the great African American leader Booker T. Washington, headlining showgirl Evelyn Nesbit, and the famed magician Harry Houdini. They each have key roles to play in this captivating saga, and in so many ways, their lives parallel the experiences of Americans and immigrants in the present day. Still subjected to soul-crushing racism and abuse, as justice is routinely granted or denied, depending on skin color. This is also a show in which the entire score deserves the highest praise. In fact, there isn’t just one 11 o’clock number, as is the standard in so many great musicals. There are several bona fide showstoppers sending audiences to their feet. Yes, the show is long at close to three hours, but it leaves you wanting more. Music has a unique way of bringing people of all stripes together, and that’s why shows like this have the power to enlighten, inspire, and remind us what we look like at our best and worst. (Music) Ragtime the Musical not only sings beautifully, it speaks to us with a relevance and a resonance that connects us all. And that’s what makes a masterpiece.
classificationReason: Roma Torre reviews the Ragtime revival at Lincoln Center's Vivian Beaumont Theater (directed by Lear deBessonet), sharing opinions on the production ('nearly flawless') and reporting on its extension. The reviewer is standing outside Lincoln Center, indicating first-hand attendance.
